concepts: Binomial expansion: coefficients of a product
questions.question: If the coefficients of $x^2$ and $x^3$ are both zero, in the expansion of the expression $(1+ax+bx^2)(1-3x)^{15}$ in powers of $x$, then the ordered pair $(a,b)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Collect each coefficient from $(1-3x)^{15}$ with $1,\,ax,\,bx^2$ and solve the two linear equations in $a,b$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use one equation to eliminate options, then confirm the survivor with the second equation.
solution: Only the $x^2$ condition is needed to filter: $945-45a+b=0$.

useful_results: For a product $P(x)\,(1+u)^n$ with a short polynomial $P$, the coefficient of $x^k$ is $\sum_j p_j\,[x^{k-j}](1+u)^n$: only $\deg P+1$ terms are needed.
With options, a single easy equation (here the $x^2$ one) usually kills three options; verify the survivor with the second equation.

concepts: Binomial expansion: general term and coefficient condition
questions.question: The smallest natural number $n$, such that the coefficient of $x$ in the expansion of $\left(x^2+\frac1{x^3}\right)^n$ is ${}^nC_{23}$, is:
questions.key_idea: ${}^nC_r={}^nC_{23}$ forces $r=23$ or $n-r=23$; each case, together with $2n-5r=1$, fixes $n$.
solution: Given that the coefficient is ${}^nC_r={}^nC_{23}$, so $r=23$ or $n-r=23$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A congruence filter: $5r=2n-1$ forces $n\equiv3\pmod5$, which leaves very few $n$ to test.

useful_results: For $\left(ax^p+\frac b{x^q}\right)^n$ the general term is ${}^nC_r\,a^{n-r}b^r\,x^{p(n-r)-qr}$; the exponent is linear in $r$, so the integrality of $r$ gives a congruence on $n$.
${}^nC_a={}^nC_b\iff a=b$ or $a+b=n$ (for $0\le a,b\le n$): the source of the two cases.
Always check the smaller candidate satisfies $0\le r\le n$ before accepting it.

concepts: Binomial expansion: coefficient in a product of polynomials
questions.question: The coefficient of $x^{18}$ in the product $(1+x)(1-x)^{10}(1+x+x^2)^9$ is:
questions.key_idea: $(1-x)(1+x+x^2)=1-x^3$ turns the product into $(1-x^3)^9(1-x^2)$.
solution: Coefficient of $x^{18}$ = (coefficient of $x^{18}$ in $(1-x^3)^9$) $-$ (coefficient of $x^{16}$ in $(1-x^3)^9$).
$(1-x^3)^9$ has only powers $x^{3j}$; $16$ is not a multiple of $3$, so the second coefficient is $0$.
useful_results: $(1-x)(1+x+\cdots+x^{m-1})=1-x^m$; with $m=3$ this collapses $(1-x)^9(1+x+x^2)^9$ into $(1-x^3)^9$. Look for such a pairing whenever $(1-x)$ and $(1+x+x^2)$ appear with matching exponents.
$[x^k](1-x^m)^n$ is $0$ unless $m\mid k$, and equals $(-1)^{k/m}\,{}^nC_{k/m}$ otherwise.
A factor $x^s$ times a polynomial in $x^m$ contributes to $x^k$ only when $m\mid(k-s)$: a quick divisibility test.

concepts: Binomial coefficient identities and summation
questions.question: If ${}^{20}C_1+(2^2)\,{}^{20}C_2+(3^2)\,{}^{20}C_3+\cdots+(20^2)\,{}^{20}C_{20}=A(2^\beta)$, then the ordered pair $(A,\beta)$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: Use $r\,{}^nC_r=n\,{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}$ twice (writing $r=(r-1)+1$) to reduce $\sum r^2\,{}^{20}C_r$ to $\sum{}^{19}C_{r}$-type sums.
useful_results: Absorption identity: $r\,{}^nC_r=n\,{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}$.
Probabilistic reading: $\sum f(r)\,{}^nC_r=2^n E[f(X)]$ with $X\sim B(n,\frac12)$; $E[X]=\frac n2$, $\operatorname{Var}X=\frac n4$.

concepts: Term independent of $x$ in a binomial expansion
questions.question: The term independent of $x$ in expansion of $\left(\frac1{60}-\frac{x^8}{81}\right)\left(2x^2-\frac3{x^2}\right)^6$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: Split the product: the constant term needs $x^0$ with $\frac1{60}$ and $x^{-8}$ with $-\frac{x^8}{81}$ from the sixth power.
solution: Coefficient of $x^0$ in the product = $\frac1{60}\times$ (coefficient of $x^0$ in $(\cdot)^6$) $-\frac1{81}\times$ (coefficient of $x^{-8}$ in $(\cdot)^6$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Clear the negative powers: $\left(2x^2-\frac3{x^2}\right)^6=\frac{(2x^4-3)^6}{x^{12}}$, so the question becomes picking powers of $v=x^4$.
solution: The product is $\left(\frac1{60}-\frac{x^8}{81}\right)x^{-12}(2v-3)^6$. The first part is constant when $x^{-12}v^j$ has $4j=12$, i.e. $j=3$.
The second part is $-\frac1{81}x^{8-12}v^j=-\frac1{81}x^{4j-4}$, constant when $j=1$.

useful_results: If every exponent in a binomial is even (or a multiple of $m$), substitute $v=x^m$ to turn the problem into counting $v$-powers.
For $\left(ax^p+\frac b{x^q}\right)^n$ the exponents are $p(n-r)-qr$; here $p=q=2$, $n=6$ gives $12-4r$, so only exponents $\equiv0\pmod4$ occur.
For $P(x)\,Q(x)^n$, a constant term is $\sum_j p_j\,[x^{-j}]Q^n$: list the exponents of $P$ and match them one by one (a parity or divisibility check often kills terms).

concepts: Divisibility and geometric progression sum
questions.question: The greatest positive integer $k$, for which $49^k+1$ is a factor of the sum $49^{125}+49^{124}+\cdots+49^2+49+1$, is:
solution: $\frac{49^{63}-1}{49-1}=1+49+\cdots+49^{62}$ is an integer, so $49^{63}+1$ divides the sum: $k=63$ works.
Maximality: if $49^k+1$ divides the sum, it divides $49^{126}-1$ (as $48\cdot$ sum), and $49^k+1\mid49^{2k}-1$ gives order of $49$ mod $49^k+1$ equal to $2k$, which must divide $126$.
So $k\mid63$, hence $k\le63$ and the greatest is $k=63$.
questions.correction_note: PDF stops at the factorisation and states k=63 without showing why no larger k works (the option 65 is excluded only by the order argument added in the last two bullets). Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the $126$ terms into two halves of $63$: the sum factors as $(1+49^{63})(1+49+\cdots+49^{62})$ with no formula needed.
solution: So $49^{63}+1$ is a factor and $k=63$ works.
Why not more: $49^k+1$ with $k>63$ would have to divide $49^{126}-1$ and so $2k\mid126$ (order argument); e.g. $k=65$ fails. Hence $k=63$.

useful_results: $1+a+\cdots+a^{2m-1}=(1+a^m)(1+a+\cdots+a^{m-1})$: a G.P. with an even number of terms splits into halves.
$a^k+1\mid a^n-1$ (for $a>1$) iff $n$ is an even multiple of $k$, i.e. $2k\mid n$; more generally $a^m-1\mid a^n-1\iff m\mid n$.
Quick check of the identity: $a=2$, $m=2$: $1+2+4+8=15=(1+4)(1+2)$.

concepts: Binomial coefficients and integer solutions
questions.question: The number of ordered pairs $(r,k)$ for which $6\cdot{}^{35}C_r=(k^2-3)\cdot{}^{36}C_{r+1}$, where $k$ is an integer, is:
questions.key_idea: ${}^{36}C_{r+1}=\frac{36}{r+1}\,{}^{35}C_r$ reduces the equation to $r+1=6(k^2-3)$ with $0\le r\le35$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes 'k=2 => r=+/-5' (and 'k=-2 => r=5'); r=6k^2-19 gives r=5 for k=+/-2, and r=-5 is impossible. Count of 4 pairs unchanged; verified by brute force.

alternate_solutions.idea: Bound the integer $\frac{r+1}{6}=k^2-3$ first, then find perfect squares.
solution: $r+1\in\{1,\dots,36\}$ and must be a multiple of $6$, so $k^2-3=\frac{r+1}6\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$.
Hence $k^2\in\{4,5,6,7,8,9\}$; only $4$ and $9$ are perfect squares.

useful_results: ${}^{n+1}C_{r+1}=\frac{n+1}{r+1}\,{}^nC_r$ (and ${}^nC_{r+1}=\frac{n-r}{r+1}\,{}^nC_r$): ratio of consecutive binomial coefficients turns a coefficient equation into an algebraic one.
The range $0\le r\le n$ is part of the problem: always use it to bound the integer unknown before testing values.
Pairs with $\pm k$ come in twos when only $k^2$ appears.

concepts: Binomial expansion with surds: even/odd terms
questions.question: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^2$ respectively in the expansion of $\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^6+\left(x-\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^6$, then:
questions.key_idea: $(a+b)^6+(a-b)^6$ keeps only the even powers of $b=\sqrt{x^2-1}$, so every surd disappears.
questions.correction_note: PDF labels the coefficient -96 as 'Coefficient of x^2 (alpha)'; -96 is the coefficient of x^4 (alpha) and 36 that of x^2 (beta). Values and answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $x=\cos\theta$: the expression is $2\cos6\theta=2T_6(x)$, a Chebyshev polynomial.
solution: Since both sides are polynomials in $x$ they agree for all $x$: $\alpha=-96$, $\beta=36$, $\alpha-\beta=-132$.

useful_results: $(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})^n+(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})^n=2T_n(x)$, the Chebyshev polynomial, with $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos n\theta$; $T_6=32x^6-48x^4+18x^2-1$.
$(a+b)^n+(a-b)^n$ contains only even powers of $b$; $(a+b)^n-(a-b)^n$ only odd powers: the standard way to remove surds.
Coefficient check: $T_n(1)=1$: $32-48+18-1=1$.

concepts: Term independent of $x$ in a binomial expansion
Range of $\sin 2\theta$
questions.question: In the expansion of $\left(\frac{x}{\cos\theta}+\frac1{x\sin\theta}\right)^{16}$, if $l_1$ is the least value of the term independent of $x$ when $\frac\pi8\le\theta\le\frac\pi4$ and $l_2$ is the least value of the term independent of $x$ when $\frac\pi{16}\le\theta\le\frac\pi8$, then the ratio $l_2:l_1$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The $x$-free term is $\frac{{}^{16}C_8\,2^8}{\sin^82\theta}$, minimal where $\sin2\theta$ is largest on the interval.
solution: For $\frac\pi8\le\theta\le\frac\pi4$: $\frac\pi4\le2\theta\le\frac\pi2$; $\sin2\theta$ is at most $1$, so the least term is $l_1={}^{16}C_8\times2^8$.
useful_results: $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac12\sin2\theta$ turns products of reciprocal trig terms into a single function of $2\theta$; remember the interval for $2\theta$ is double the interval for $\theta$.
$\sin2\theta$ is increasing for $2\theta\in[0,\frac\pi2]$ and decreasing afterwards, so on a given interval its extremes sit at an end point or at $2\theta=\frac\pi2$.
Term independent of $x$ in $(ax+\frac bx)^{2m}$ is ${}^{2m}C_m(ab)^m$; here $ab=\frac1{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$.

concepts: Binomial coefficient sums with alternating signs
Differentiation of the binomial expansion
questions.question: The value of $-{}^{15}C_1+2\cdot{}^{15}C_2-3\cdot{}^{15}C_3+\cdots-15\cdot{}^{15}C_{15}+{}^{14}C_1+{}^{14}C_3+{}^{14}C_5+\cdots+{}^{14}C_{11}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Differentiate $(1+x)^{15}$ and put $x=-1$ to kill the alternating part; the odd-index sum of ${}^{14}C_r$ is $2^{13}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Absorption identity $r\,{}^nC_r=n\,{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}$ turns the alternating sum into $15(1-1)^{14}$.
solution: The given alternating part $-{}^{15}C_1+2\cdot{}^{15}C_2-\cdots-15\cdot{}^{15}C_{15}$ is exactly $\sum_{r=1}^{15}(-1)^r\,r\,{}^{15}C_r=0$.
Odd-size subsets: ${}^{14}C_1+{}^{14}C_3+\cdots+{}^{14}C_{13}$ counts the odd-size subsets of a $14$-set, which are exactly half of $2^{14}$, i.e. $2^{13}$.

useful_results: $\sum_{r}(-1)^r\,r\,{}^nC_r=0$ for $n\ge2$ (it is $-1$ for $n=1$); more generally $\sum(-1)^r\,r^j\,{}^nC_r=0$ for $0\le j<n$.
Differentiating $(1+x)^n$ and putting $x=\pm1$ is the standard route for sums with a factor $r$ in front.
Watch the number of terms: the last term of an incomplete odd-index sum may need to be subtracted (here ${}^{14}C_{13}$).

concepts: Summation of binomial coefficients ${}^kC_2$ (hockey stick)
questions.question: If $n\ge2$ is a positive integer, then the sum of the series ${}^{n+1}C_2+2\left({}^2C_2+{}^3C_2+{}^4C_2+\cdots+{}^nC_2\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: The hockey-stick identity gives ${}^2C_2+{}^3C_2+\cdots+{}^nC_2={}^{n+1}C_3$.
useful_results: Hockey stick: $\sum_{k=r}^{n}{}^kC_r={}^{n+1}C_{r+1}$.
$k^2=2\,{}^kC_2+{}^kC_1$, so $\sum_{k=1}^nk^2=2\,{}^{n+1}C_3+{}^{n+1}C_2$: the bridge between powers and binomial coefficients.
$k^3=6\,{}^kC_3+6\,{}^kC_2+{}^kC_1$ gives $\sum k^3$ the same way.

concepts: Term independent of $t$ in a binomial expansion
Maxima of a function (AM-GM)
questions.question: The maximum value of the term independent of '$t$' in the expansion of $\left(tx^{1/5}+\frac{(1-x)^{1/10}}{t}\right)^{10}$ where $x\in(0,1)$ is:
questions.key_idea: The $t$-free term is the middle term ${}^{10}C_5\,x\sqrt{1-x}$; maximise it on $(0,1)$.
solution: The term independent of $t$ is the middle term ($r=5$), where $t^5\cdot t^{-5}=1$.
$f(0^+)=f(1^-)=0$ and $f>0$ inside, so $x=\frac23$ is the point of maximum.

alternate_solutions.idea: Maximise $x^2(1-x)$ by weighted AM-GM instead of differentiating: write it as $4\cdot\frac x2\cdot\frac x2\cdot(1-x)$.
solution: $x^2(1-x)=4\cdot\frac x2\cdot\frac x2\cdot(1-x)\le4\left(\frac{\frac x2+\frac x2+1-x}3\right)^3=4\cdot\frac1{27}$ (the three factors have constant sum $1$).

useful_results: In $\left(at+\frac bt\right)^{2m}$ the $t$-free term is the middle term ${}^{2m}C_m(ab)^m$.
Weighted AM-GM: to maximise $x^p(1-x)^q$ write it as a product of $p+q$ equal-sum factors: maximum at $x=\frac p{p+q}$; here $p=2,q=1$ gives $\frac23$.
Check of the answer: $252\cdot\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}\approx96.99$, matching a direct scan of $252\,x\sqrt{1-x}$.

concepts: Even and odd coefficients of a polynomial (evaluation at $\pm1$)
questions.question: Let $[x]$ denote greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. If for $n\in\mathbb N$, $(1-x+x^3)^n=\sum_{j=0}^{3n}a_jx^j$, then $\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor3n/2\rfloor}a_{2j}+4\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor(3n-1)/2\rfloor}a_{2j+1}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The two sums are the sums of the even-indexed and odd-indexed coefficients of $f(x)=(1-x+x^3)^n$: use $f(1)$ and $f(-1)$.
solution: Let $f(x)=(1-x+x^3)^n$. The floor limits cover exactly all even indices $0\le2j\le3n$ and all odd indices $1\le2j+1\le3n$.
useful_results: For $f(x)=\sum a_jx^j$: $\sum a_{2j}=\frac{f(1)+f(-1)}2$ and $\sum a_{2j+1}=\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}2$.
Reading the limits: $\lfloor\frac{N}{2}\rfloor$ and $\lfloor\frac{N-1}2\rfloor$ are just the largest allowed even and odd indices for degree $N$.
Weighted combos such as $\sum a_{even}+4\sum a_{odd}=\frac{5f(1)-3f(-1)}2$; here it equals $\frac{5-3}{2}=1$.

concepts: Binomial coefficient identities: sum of squares (Vandermonde)
questions.question: If $\left({}^{30}C_1\right)^2+2\left({}^{30}C_2\right)^2+3\left({}^{30}C_3\right)^2+\cdots+30\left({}^{30}C_{30}\right)^2=\frac{\alpha\,60!}{(30!)^2}$, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Reverse the order of the sum ($r\to30-r$) and add: $2S=30\sum\left({}^{30}C_r\right)^2=30\,{}^{60}C_{30}$.

solution: $\sum_{r=1}^{30}{}^{29}C_{r-1}\,{}^{30}C_{30-r}$: the lower indices add to $29$, so by Vandermonde this is ${}^{59}C_{29}$.

useful_results: $\sum_r\left({}^nC_r\right)^2={}^{2n}C_n$; reversing the index ($r\to n-r$) and adding is the quick way to handle a linear weight $r$.
Vandermonde: $\sum_r{}^mC_r\,{}^nC_{k-r}={}^{m+n}C_k$.

concepts: Ratio of consecutive binomial coefficients and power sums
questions.question: If $a_r$ is the coefficient of $x^{10-r}$ in the Binomial expansion of $(1+x)^{10}$, then $\sum_{r=1}^{10}r^3\left(\frac{a_r}{a_{r-1}}\right)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\frac{a_r}{a_{r-1}}=\frac{11-r}{r}$, so the summand simplifies to $r(11-r)^2$, a cubic in $r$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the sums from r=0, but the given sum starts at r=1 (a_{-1} is undefined). The r=0 term of r(11-r)^2 is 0, so the value 1210 is unchanged; written here from r=1.
useful_results: $\frac{{}^nC_r}{{}^nC_{r-1}}=\frac{n-r+1}r$: the ratio of consecutive binomial coefficients is linear fractional in $r$, so powers of $r$ often cancel.
$\sum_{r=1}^nr=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, $\ \sum r^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$, $\ \sum r^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2$.
For a sum over $1..N$ symmetric under $r\to N+1-r$, adding the sum to its reversal often makes it a multiple of a simpler sum.

concepts: Binomial expansion: odd-power coefficients and middle term
questions.question: Let $K$ be the sum of the coefficients of the odd powers of $x$ in the expansion of $(1+x)^{99}$. Let $a$ be the middle term in the expansion of $\left(2+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^{200}$. If $\frac{{}^{200}C_{99}\,K}{a}=\frac{2^\ell m}n$, where $m$ and $n$ are odd numbers, then the ordered pair $(\ell,n)$ is equal to
solution: The expansion of $\left(2+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^{200}$ has $201$ terms, so the middle term is $T_{101}$.
useful_results: The sum of coefficients of the odd powers of $(1+x)^N$ equals $2^{N-1}$ for $N\ge1$.
Writing a number as $2^\ell\cdot\frac mn$ with $m,n$ odd is just extracting its $2$-adic valuation $\ell$ (here Kummer's theorem also works: $v_2\left({}^{200}C_{99}\right)=5$).

concepts: Geometric progression of binomial terms
questions.question: The coefficient of $x^{301}$ in $(1+x)^{500}+x(1+x)^{499}+x^2(1+x)^{498}+\cdots+x^{500}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The terms form a G.P. with ratio $\frac x{1+x}$ whose sum is $(1+x)^{501}-x^{501}$.
solution: The sum has $501$ terms, first term $(1+x)^{500}$ and common ratio $\frac x{1+x}$.
Coefficient of $x^{301}$ in $(1+x)^{501}-x^{501}$: the term $x^{501}$ contributes nothing to $x^{301}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count term by term and apply the hockey-stick identity.

useful_results: $\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^k(1+x)^{n-k}=(1+x)^{n+1}-x^{n+1}$ (G.P. of $n+1$ terms with ratio $\frac x{1+x}$).
Hockey stick: $\sum_{m=r}^{n}{}^mC_r={}^{n+1}C_{r+1}$.
For $k<n+1$ the subtracted $x^{n+1}$ never affects the coefficient of $x^k$.

concepts: Binomial expansion with surds
Greatest integer function (integral part and parity)
questions.question: Let $x=\left(8\sqrt3+13\right)^{13}$ and $y=\left(7\sqrt2+9\right)^9$. If $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer $\le t$, then
questions.key_idea: $x-x'$ is an even integer for the conjugate $x'=(8\sqrt3-13)^{13}$, and $0<x'<1$, so $[x]=x-x'$.
solution: $x-x'=2\left[{}^{13}C_1(8\sqrt3)^{12}13+{}^{13}C_3(8\sqrt3)^{10}13^3+\cdots\right]$: only even powers of $8\sqrt3$ occur, which are integers, so $x-x'$ is an even integer.
Hence $x=(x-x')+x'$ has integer part $[x]=x-x'$, which is even.
Similarly $y=(7\sqrt2+9)^9$ and $y'=(7\sqrt2-9)^9$: $y-y'=2\left[{}^9C_1(7\sqrt2)^8\cdot9+{}^9C_3(7\sqrt2)^6\cdot9^3+\cdots\right]$ is an even integer.
Both $[x]$ and $[y]$ are even, so $[x]+[y]$ is even: option $(B)$.
questions.correction_note: PDF concludes '[x] is even' from 'x - x' is an even integer' without proving 0 < x' < 1 (needed for [x] = x - x'); same for y. The two bounding bullets were added. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Power sums satisfy a recurrence $T_n=sT_{n-1}-pT_{n-2}$ whose parity is constant; the conjugate power is negative and small.
solution: Mod $2$: $T_n\equiv T_{n-2}$, and $T_0,T_1$ are even, so every $T_n$ is even; in particular $T_{13}$ is an even integer.

useful_results: For $a>0$ and $a<\sqrt b<a+1$: $T_n=(\sqrt b+a)^n+(a-\sqrt b)^n$ is an integer, and for odd $n$ the conjugate power $(a-\sqrt b)^n\in(-1,0)$, so $\left[(\sqrt b+a)^n\right]=T_n$.
The standard device: $(p+q)^n\pm(p-q)^n$ keeps only even (or only odd) powers of $q$, so surds vanish; always verify $|p-q|<1$.
Recurrence for $T_n=u^n+v^n$: $T_n=(u+v)T_{n-1}-uv\,T_{n-2}$; it makes parity or divisibility checks immediate.

concepts: Sum of odd-indexed binomial coefficients
questions.question: The value of $\frac1{1!\,50!}+\frac1{3!\,48!}+\frac1{5!\,46!}+\cdots+\frac1{49!\,2!}+\frac1{51!\,1!}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Each term is $\frac{1}{i!\,(51-i)!}=\frac{{}^{51}C_i}{51!}$ with $i$ odd, so the sum is the odd-index binomial sum $2^{50}$ over $51!$.
solution: The general term is $\frac1{(2r-1)!\,(51-(2r-1))!}$ for $r=1,\dots,26$ (the last term has $51!$ with $0!=1!=1$).
Sum of odd-indexed binomial coefficients of $(1+x)^{51}$ is $2^{50}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Generating functions: the sum is the coefficient of $x^{51}$ in $\sinh x\cdot e^x=\frac{e^{2x}-1}2$.
solution: $\sinh x=\sum_{i\text{ odd}}\frac{x^i}{i!}$ and $e^x=\sum_j\frac{x^j}{j!}$, so $[x^{51}]\,\sinh x\,e^x=\sum_{i\text{ odd}}\frac1{i!\,(51-i)!}$, the required sum.

useful_results: $\frac1{i!\,(n-i)!}=\frac{{}^nC_i}{n!}$: a sum of reciprocal factorial pairs with $i+j=n$ is a binomial sum divided by $n!$.
Odd-index and even-index binomial sums are both $2^{n-1}$ ($n\ge1$).
The last term $\frac1{51!\,1!}$ equals $\frac1{51!\,0!}$ numerically, so the printed $1!$ does not change the value.

concepts: Exponential series ($\cosh1$, $\sinh1$) and summation
questions.question: The sum $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2n^2+3n+4}{(2n)!}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write the numerator as $2n(2n-1)+8n+8$ (twice the given one) so each part cancels into $\frac1{(2n-2)!},\frac1{(2n-1)!},\frac1{(2n)!}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Operator method: with $\theta=x\frac d{dx}$, $\ n\to\frac\theta2$ acting on $\cosh x=\sum\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$.
solution: $\theta\cosh x=x\sinh x$ and $\theta^2\cosh x=x\sinh x+x^2\cosh x$; at $x=1$: $\theta F=\sinh1$, $\theta^2F=\sinh1+\cosh1=e$.

useful_results: Strategy for $\sum\frac{P(n)}{m!}$: rewrite $P$ in falling factorials $m(m-1),\,m,\,1$ so that each term cancels into a plain factorial.
$\frac{m(m-1)}{m!}=\frac1{(m-2)!}$ and $\frac m{m!}=\frac1{(m-1)!}$.
Remember the sum starts at $n=1$: subtract the $n=0$ term, e.g. $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{(2n)!}=\cosh1-1$.
